#### 1. hypermethioninemia with deficiency of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.435)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-156581, Reactome:R-HSA-1614635, Reactome:R-HSA-2408508)

**Proposed mechanism:** MAT1A (HGNC:6929) —PRODUCES→ S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:16870); Methionine (CHEBI:17790) —INCREASES→ S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:16870); S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:16870) —LEADS_TO→ Methionine metabolism (R-HSA-168700); Methionine metabolism (R-HSA-168700) —LEADS_TO→ Developmental delay (HP:0001263); AHCY (HGNC:244) —PRODUCES→ S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17636); S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:16870) —DISRUPTS→ S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17636); S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17636) —LEADS_TO→ S-adenosylhomocysteine metabolism (R-HSA-195404); S-adenosylhomocysteine metabolism (R-HSA-195404) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:16870) —LEADS_TO→ S-adenosylhomocysteine metabolism (R-HSA-195404). Loss-of-function mutations in MAT1A lead to decreased production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), a critical methyl donor. Concurrently, loss-of-function mutations in AHCY impair the hydrolysis of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), leading to its accumulation and feedback inhibition of SAM-dependent methyltransferases. Both altered SAM levels and SAH accumulation disrupt essential metabolic pathways, ultimately contributing to developmental delay and intellectual disability.

**How to falsify it:** If mutations in MAT1A or AHCY are found to be gain-of-function or dominant-negative in nature, or if the shared phenotypes (developmental delay, intellectual disability) are not observed in individuals with documented loss-of-function mutations in both genes, this mechanistic link would be falsified. _(variant: Presence of common pathogenic variants in MAT1A or AHCY (e.g., allele frequency > 1% in gnomAD) would challenge their role as rare disease-causing genes.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding this shared metabolic pathway disruption is crucial for developing targeted therapies. Interventions aimed at restoring SAM/SAH balance or mitigating downstream effects of their dysregulation could potentially benefit patients with either condition.

Concurrently, loss-of-function mutations in CBS impair the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine, leading to homocysteine accumulation and disruption of methionine metabolism, which underlies phenotypes such as intellectual disability and thrombosis.
